answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This is Alcott's own line — spoken by the character Amy in Little Women, Part Second, Chapter 44 (1869). The popular version swaps her contractions (“I'm”) for the fuller “I am,” a minor but documented misquotation.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Little Women, Part Second (“Good Wives”), Ch. 44: “My Lord and Lady”
April 1869 (Part First: 30 September 1868), Roberts Brothers, Boston
Amy (March) Laurence, newly married, to her family

source.excerpt: Lovely weather so far; I don't know how long it will last, but I'm not afraid of storms, for I'm learning how to sail my ship. Come home, dear, and I'll find your bootjack; I suppose that's what you are rummaging after among my things. Men are so helpless, mother.
trail: The line is spoken by Amy, newly married to Laurie, in Part Second, Chapter 44, “My Lord and Lady,” per the full chapter text at Wikisource ↗.
Wikiquote's Alcott page lists the same passage and explicitly flags that it is “sometimes...slightly misquoted” with “I am” replacing the novel's “I'm,” per Wikiquote ↗.
Part Second of Little Women was first published in April 1869, about three months after Part First appeared on 30 September 1868, per Wikipedia ↗.
source.excerptNote: Alcott's original text uses contractions (“I'm”), not the “I am” form most often quoted online.
source.rightsNote: Little Women was first published in 1868–69 by Roberts Brothers, decades before the 1931 U.S. public-domain cutoff, so the novel and this line are in the public domain in the United States.

author.bio: Louisa May Alcott was an American novelist raised among New England transcendentalists, best known for the semi-autobiographical Little Women (1868–69) and its sequels. Beyond her celebrated domestic fiction she also wrote sensation thrillers under a pseudonym and was an active abolitionist and suffragist.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: The credit to Louisa May Alcott is correct — she wrote this line — but two details are commonly lost in circulation: it is spoken by the character Amy, not stated as Alcott's own personal maxim, and the wording is slightly altered from the original.

items.why: Alcott's text reads “I'm not afraid of storms, for I'm learning how to sail my ship” (contractions), not the widely shared “I am not afraid of storms, for I am learning how to sail my ship.” Wikiquote explicitly labels this a “slightly misquoted” variant, per Wikiquote ↗.
Despite Jo being the novel's most quoted character, this particular line belongs to Amy, addressing her family after her marriage to Laurie, per the chapter text at Wikisource ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Alcott really wrote this line in Little Women (1869); it's Amy's reassurance to her family about married life, and the version usually shared online swaps her contractions for the fuller “I am,” per Wikisource ↗.

context.heading: Amy's answer to an uncertain future
lead: By the novel's end, Amy March — once the family's most self-absorbed sister — has married her childhood friend Laurie and settled into adult married life. When her family teases the newlyweds about what comes next, Amy answers with quiet confidence: she doesn't know how long the good weather will last, but she isn't afraid of storms, because she is learning to sail her own ship.

The line has since been lifted out of that domestic scene and circulated as a stand-alone motivational maxim, usually without noting that it belongs to Amy rather than to Alcott speaking in her own voice, or to Jo, the character most associated with grit in the novel.
